content: 1. When specific data is unavailable, the total population can be used as the denominator for estimation purposes. 2. Indicator SI 18 measures the percentage of hearing aid users who receive regular maintenance and follow-up services, expressed as a percentage of those fitted with hearing aids. This data is typically collected annually through government reports and hearing aid providers. 3. Indicator SI 19 evaluates the percentage of hearing aid users who report an improved quality of life during follow-up, expressed as a percentage of those fitted with hearing aids. This assessment is conducted once every 10 years using survey questionnaires as part of population-based surveys. 4. The total number of individuals fitted with hearing aids and/or cochlear implants can be calculated as a percentage of the total number of people with hearing loss, or as a ratio of the total population of the country per 100,000 individuals. 5. Supplementary Indicator 14 focuses on the number of children aged 0–15 fitted with hearing aids and/or cochlear implants, expressed as a percentage of children with hearing loss or as a ratio of the population aged 0–15 per 100,000 individuals. 6. Supplementary Indicator 15 measures the number of individuals aged 15–60 fitted with hearing aids and/or cochlear implants, expressed as a percentage of persons aged 15–60 with hearing loss, or as a ratio of the population aged 15–60 per 100,000 individuals. 7. Supplementary Indicator 16 evaluates the number of individuals above 60 years of age fitted with hearing aids and/or cochlear implants, expressed as a percentage of persons above 60 with hearing loss, or as a ratio of the population above 60 per 100,000 individuals. 8. Indicator SI 17 measures the number of individuals receiving cochlear implants as a percentage of persons with hearing loss, or as a ratio of the population per 100,000 individuals. Data can be sourced from government departments or cochlear implant distributors. 9. Supplementary Indicator 18 assesses the percentage of hearing aid users who receive regular maintenance and follow-up services, expressed as a percentage of those fitted with hearing aids. This indicator is relevant in settings where follow-up services are provided by government or NGO-led hearing service providers. 10. Supplementary Indicator 19 evaluates the percentage of hearing aid users who report an improved quality of life during follow-up, expressed as a percentage of those fitted with hearing aids. This assessment should be conducted at least once every 10 years through questionnaire-based surveys or as part of population-based prevalence studies. 11. Core Indicator 11 measures the budget allocated for implementing the national strategy on hearing care as a percentage of the total health budget. This information is typically found in financial planning documents and ministry reports. 12. Supplementary Indicator 20 evaluates the budget allocated for the office of the Ear and Hearing Care (EHC) coordinator as a percentage of the total health budget. This data is also found in financial planning documents and ministry reports. 13. Supplementary Indicator 21 calculates the per capita expenditure on ear and hearing care services, expressed in both national currency and US dollars. This information is derived from financial planning documents and ministry reports. 14. Core Indicator 12 ensures that indicators for ear and hearing care are included in the government-led health information system (HIS) of the country. This data can be sourced from the Ministry of Health and its reports. 15. Core Indicator 13 measures the prevalence of hearing loss as a percentage of the population, disaggregated by severity, type, etiology, age, and gender. This data is collected through population-based surveys conducted at least once every 10 years. 16. Core Indicator 14 evaluates the prevalence of ear diseases, such as otitis media, as a percentage of the population, disaggregated by type, age, and gender. This data is also collected through population-based surveys conducted at least once every 10 years. 17. Data on hearing loss and ear diseases should be gathered periodically to monitor trends and assess the effectiveness of public health strategies. This data collection should include hearing tests and ear examinations, following the WHO Ear and Hearing Survey Handbook. 18. Cochlear implant companies maintain records on the number and types of cochlear implants fitted in the country. This information can be obtained from manufacturers or through discussions with health authorities. 19. Policies on occupational noise control, hearing aid provision, and ototoxicity monitoring can be sourced from relevant authorities such as occupational health divisions, industry regulatory agencies, and departments of health or medicine. 20. Government reports provide regular updates on departmental activities, human resource availability, and initiatives. When relevant information is missing, dialogue with concerned departments is necessary to advocate for its inclusion. 21. Hearing aid providers can supply data on follow-up services for hearing aid users when such information is not available from government sources. 22. Implementation reports from state, district, or field-level organizations document activities such as hearing screening, hearing aid services, and training programs. These reports should be standardized and included in national strategies. 23. National annual health reports issued by the Ministry of Health document key health indices and should include relevant ear and hearing care indicators. 24. Reports from national associations of ENT specialists and audiological professionals can provide information on human resource availability when other sources are lacking. 25. Hospital reports contain data on programs implemented at the facility level, such as diagnosis, audiological tests, and hearing aid services. These reports should be standardized and included in national strategies. 26. Reports from national committee meetings or planning sessions organized by the Ministry of Health can provide insights into ear and hearing care initiatives. 27. Reports from NGOs involved in ear and hearing care services or training can serve as valuable sources of information. 28. School health reports in areas with active school health programs should include relevant ear and hearing care indicators. Standardized formats should be developed for inclusion in these reports. 29. Standard treatment guidelines issued by the government assist practitioners and patients in making decisions about appropriate healthcare for specific clinical circumstances. These guidelines can include policies on monitoring ototoxic medications. 30. Training implementation reports from countries conducting specialized courses for primary-level physicians and community health workers in ear and hearing care can provide valuable data.
